sections.title: Qualities of youth & generation gap
sections.content:
# Qualities of youth (noun → adjective)
• **imagination** → imaginative: forming pictures and ideas in your mind
• **talent / gift** → talented / gifted: a natural ability or skill
• **adventure** → adventurous: loving exciting experiences and risks
• **ambition** → ambitious: having big dreams and working to achieve them
• **passion** → passionate: a strong feeling of love for something
• **creativity** → creative: making new things, using original ideas
• **punctuality** → punctual: respecting time, never late
• **vitality** → vital / energetic: a great deal of energy

# Negative qualities
• **carelessness** → careless: not paying attention, causing problems
• **immaturity** → immature: acting like a child, not responsible
• **impatience** → impatient: hating to wait
• **aggressiveness** → aggressive: tending toward violence

# Generation gap
The **generation gap** is the difference in ideas, values and lifestyle between young and old people, which causes misunderstandings.
• Young people may think old people are: **old-fashioned**, **severe** (too serious, strict), **nosy** (asking about everything), **stingy** (not liking to spend money).
• Old people may think young people are: **irresponsible**, **thoughtless** (not thinking about others or consequences), **strong-headed** / **obstinate** (sticking to their opinions).

sections.title: Gerund & infinitive
sections.content:
# Gerund (verb + -ing)
Use a **gerund**:
• as the **subject** of a sentence: **Dancing** is an excellent activity.
• after **prepositions**: interested in **learning**, apologize for **being** late, before **leaving**, without **making** mistakes, look forward to **meeting**.
• after these verbs: enjoy, finish, avoid, admit, deny, consider, imagine, miss, practise, keep, mind, suggest, risk, discuss.
• after expressions: can't stand, can't help, can't resist, feel like, it's no use, there's no point in, would you mind.

# Infinitive (to + verb)
Use a **to-infinitive**:
• after these verbs: want, decide, promise, refuse, agree, need, hope, pretend, plan, wish, expect, learn, afford, manage, attempt.
• after **adjectives**: It's easy **to say**; I was surprised **to see** you.
• after **question words**: I don't know **what to do**; she knows **how to make** pizza.

# Bare infinitive (verb without “to”)
• after **modals**: can, could, must, should, will, would, may, might — You should **visit** a doctor.
• after **let, make, help**: Her story made everyone **cry**. Let me **speak**.
• after **had better** and **would rather**: You had better **apologize**.

# Verbs followed by both
• Same meaning: like, love, hate, prefer, start, begin, continue (I like **cooking** = I like **to cook**).
• Different meaning:
• **stop** smoking = quit the habit / **stop to** smoke = stop in order to smoke
• **remember / forget doing** = a memory of the past / **remember / forget to do** = a task you must do

sections.content:
# Making requests
• Could you please + infinitive …?
• Can you please + infinitive …?
• Could you possibly + infinitive …?
• Can I ask you to + infinitive …?
• Do you think you could + infinitive …?
• Would it be possible for you to + infinitive …?
• Would you be so kind as to + infinitive …?
• I wonder if you could + infinitive …
• I'd appreciate it if you could + infinitive …
• I'd like you to + infinitive …
• **Would you mind + gerund …?** (Would you mind opening the window?)

# Accepting requests
• Yes, sure. / Of course! / With pleasure! / Why not? / No problem.

# Refusing requests
• I'm awfully sorry, but … / I'm afraid I can't. / Sorry, I wish I could, but … / No, I can't.

# Tip
To answer “Would you mind …?” positively, say **“No, not at all.”** (= I don't mind, I'll do it).

sections.title: Sources of humour
sections.content:
# Sources of humour
• **jokes**: short stories that make people laugh
• **comedy films / comedy plays / sitcoms** (situation comedies on TV)
• **cartoons**: films using animation instead of real people
• **caricature**: a funny drawing that exaggerates someone's features
• **pranks**: practical jokes or tricks played on someone
• **memes / trolls**: funny images or videos shared online
• **one-man show / comedy show**

# People
• **humorist**, **comedian**, **jokes teller** (a person good at telling jokes), **caricaturist**

# Verbs
• **to laugh**, **to crack / tell a joke**
• **to kid with someone**: to have fun with someone
• **to make fun of someone**: to laugh at someone in a negative way
• **to play a prank / trick on someone**

# Adjectives
• **funny**, **amusing**
• **witty**: funny in an intelligent way
• **silly**: funny in a stupid way
• **hilarious**: extremely funny

# Collocations
• **sense of humour**: the ability to understand and enjoy jokes
• **burst into laughter**: to suddenly start laughing very hard
• **facial expressions**: movements of the face
• **black humour**: looking at serious things in an amusing way

sections.title: Present & past modals
sections.content:
# Present modals (modal + bare infinitive)
• **can**: ability (Jack can swim well) / permission (Can I use your phone?) / request (Can you help me?)
• **can't**: inability (He can't climb, his leg hurts) / impossibility (She can't be your sister; you look different)
• **could**: polite request (Could you bring me tea?) / past ability (My granny could swim)
• **couldn't**: past inability (I couldn't understand English when I was young)
• **may**: polite permission (May I open the window?) / possibility (Alex may travel tomorrow)
• **might**: possibility (It might rain later)
• **must**: obligation (People must respect the law) / certainty (She is angry. She must have problems)
• **mustn't**: prohibition (You mustn't use phones in class)
• **should / shouldn't**: advice (You look tired. You should rest)
• **have to**: obligation, often external (I have to call the doctor)
• **don't have to / needn't**: no obligation (You needn't buy milk; I bought some)
• **will**: certainty about the future · **would**: unreal situation / polite request

# Past modals (modal + have + past participle)
• **could have + pp**: possible in the past, but it didn't happen (I could have done the homework, but I was busy)
• **would have + pp**: a past intention that didn't happen (I would have visited you, but I lost your address)
• **should have + pp**: criticism or regret about the past (You should have seen a doctor)
• **might / may have + pp**: past possibility, not sure (She might have taken the wrong bus)
• **must have + pp**: logical certainty about the past (He was angry. He must have had problems)
• **can't / couldn't have + pp**: impossibility in the past (She can't have said that; she wasn't there)
• **needn't have + pp**: you did it, but it wasn't necessary

sections.title: Education & literacy
sections.content:
# Key words
• **education**: the acquisition of knowledge
• **to graduate**: to finish school or university
• **certificate / degree / diploma**: what students get when they finish their studies
• **scholarship**: money given to students to help pay for their studies
• **abroad**: outside your country
• **school fees**: money you pay to study
• **boarding school**: a school where students who live far away study and live
• **higher education**: studying at college, university or higher institutes
• **e-learning**: remote learning using computers and the internet

# School levels
• pre-school / kindergarten → primary school → middle school → secondary (high) school → higher education (university)

# Types of education
• **Formal education**: in school; sponsored by the government; obligatory (compulsory); ends with a degree. Examples: primary school, secondary school, university, college.
• **Non-formal education**: programmes in a school-like setting; not obligatory; usually not evaluated; no degree; often sponsored by associations. Examples: literacy programmes, music classes, extra hours.
• **Informal education**: unintentional; happens in daily life and work; lifelong. Examples: learning from parents, reading books, watching documentaries.

# Literacy
• **literacy**: the ability to read and write → **literate** person
• **illiteracy**: the inability to read and write → **illiterate** person
• **literacy classes / programmes**: classes that teach adults to read and write

sections.title: Past perfect simple
sections.content:
# Past perfect simple
**Form:** had + past participle
• (+) I **had learnt** some Arabic before I moved to Morocco.
• (–) She **hadn't studied** Arabic before she came.
• (?) **Had** you **studied** Arabic before you moved?

# Use
We use the past perfect for the **first** of two past actions (the earlier one). The second action is in the **past simple**.
• Lucy got her certificate. Then she worked as a manager. → After Lucy **had got** her certificate, she **worked** as a manager.
• Before John **moved** to Morocco, he **had studied** Arabic.

# Time words
• **after, as soon as, already, ever, never, just** → usually go with the **past perfect** action.
• **when, before, by the time** → usually go with the **past simple** action.
• When we arrived at the station, the train **had already left**.

• **so that + subject + can / could / will / would + verb**: Sophie attends literacy classes **so that she can read**.
• **for + noun**: Students go to school **for a diploma**.
• **for + gerund** (the purpose of a thing): A dictionary is used **for checking** words.

# Watch out
• After **in order to / so as to** use the **base form**: in order to study (NOT in order to studying).
• After **so that** use a full clause with a subject and usually a modal.
• Use **could / would** after so that when the main verb is in the past: He worked hard so that he **could** buy a car.

sections.content:
# Sustainable development
**Sustainable development** means meeting the needs of the present without harming the ability of future generations to meet their own needs. It moves us from problems to solutions, from negative to positive.
It works on three issues: **social**, **economic** and **environmental**.

# Social & economic issues (problem → solution)
• **poverty** → job opportunities, fair distribution of wealth
• **unemployment** → **job opportunities**, investment, microcredits
• **discrimination** → **social justice**, equality
• **poor healthcare** → **quality healthcare**
• **illiteracy / poor education** → **good education**

# Environmental issues (problem → solution)
• **pollution** → **recycling**, clean energy
• **global warming / climate change** → **renewable energies**: **solar energy** (sun), **wind energy** (wind), hydro energy (water)
• **deforestation** (cutting down forests) → **reforestation** (planting trees)
• **drought** (lack of rain) → saving water

# Useful words
• **to preserve / protect** the environment · **resources** · **to reduce** waste · **greenhouse gases** · **fossil fuels** (oil, coal, gas)

sections.title: Future perfect
sections.content:
# Future perfect
**Form:** will have + past participle
• (+) By 10 o'clock, he **will have finished** his work.
• (–) By 10 o'clock, he **will not (won't) have finished** his work.
• (?) **Will** he **have finished** his work by 10 o'clock?

# Use
We use the future perfect for an action that **will be completed before a certain time in the future**.
• She is a student now. By 2038, she **will have got** a job, **bought** a car and **got** married.

# Time expressions
• **by** + time (by 2030, by next year, by Monday, by the time …)
• **before** + time / clause
• **in** + period (in two years' time)

# Common mistakes
• ✗ will have not finish → ✓ will not have finished
• ✗ Will Robin has sold …? → ✓ Will Robin have sold …?
• ✗ will have sleep → ✓ will have slept

# Cause and effect
• The **cause** answers “Why?” — The **effect** (result) answers “What happened?”
• He had a toothache (cause) → He went to the dentist (effect).

# Linking words of CAUSE
• **because / since / as / for + clause**: Investment is important **because** it creates jobs.
• **because of / due to / owing to / thanks to + noun**: The drought is **due to** lack of rain. Youths can start businesses **thanks to** microcredits (positive cause).

# Linking words of EFFECT
• **so** + clause: Many young people are jobless, **so** banks must help them.
• **therefore / thus / consequently / as a result / as a consequence / because of this / for this reason** (usually at the start of a new sentence, followed by a comma):
Global warming is serious. **Therefore**, we must stop pollution.

# Watch out
• **because** + subject + verb ↔ **because of** + noun: because it rained / because of the rain.

sections.content:
# The situation of women
**In the past**, women were often:
• **illiterate** (illiteracy): could not read or write
• **silenced** (silence): not allowed to express opinions freely
• **dependent** (dependence): relying on others (men) for support
• **marginalized** (marginalization): pushed aside from society and opportunities
• had **limited career options**: could choose from very few jobs

**Today**, women are more:
• **literate** (literacy): able to read and write
• **outspoken**: freely expressing thoughts and opinions
• **independent** (independence): able to live without needing others' help
• **involved** (involvement): participating actively in society
• have **more career options**: can choose from many jobs

# Constraining obstacles
• **domestic violence**: physical or psychological abuse at home
• **male domination**: men controlling women unfairly
• **early age marriage**: marriage before adulthood
• **polygamy**: being married to more than one spouse at the same time
• **stereotypes**: fixed, often unfair ideas about a group of people

# Helping factors
• **gender equality**: equal rights and opportunities for men and women
• **the family code (Moudawana)**: laws that protect family members' rights
• **the media**: TV, newspapers, internet
• **education**
• **women's empowerment** (to empower): giving women power, confidence and the ability to make choices

sections.title: The passive voice
sections.content:
# The passive voice
We use the passive when **the action is more important than the doer**, or when **the doer is unknown or obvious**.
• Active: Feminists defend gender equality. → Passive: Gender equality **is defended** (by feminists).

# Form: object + be (in the same tense) + past participle (+ by agent)
Four steps: 1) start with the object · 2) put **be** in the tense of the active verb · 3) add the **past participle** · 4) add “by + agent” only if it is important.

# Tenses
• Present simple: They make cars in Japan → Cars **are made** in Japan.
• Present continuous: They are sending messages → Messages **are being sent**.
• Past simple: Someone stole my phone → My phone **was stolen**.
• Past continuous: He was painting my house → My house **was being painted**.
• Present perfect: Susan has fed her pets → The pets **have been fed**.
• Past perfect: Someone had stolen Kate's car → Kate's car **had been stolen**.
• Future simple: They will take the jewels → The jewels **will be taken**.
• Future perfect: We will have finished the report → The report **will have been finished**.
• Modals: They must finish the report → The report **must be finished**.

# Verbs with two objects
We sent a message to Mark → **A message was sent** to Mark / **Mark was sent** a message.

sections.title: Linking words of addition & concession
sections.content:
# Linking words of ADDITION (to add an idea)
• **and / also / too / as well as**: Women are marginalized **and** dependent.
• **In addition, / Moreover, / Furthermore, / Additionally, / Besides, / In addition to this,** + new sentence:
In the past, women were silenced. **Moreover**, they were marginalized.
• **in addition to / along with / besides + noun or gerund**: **In addition to** being silenced, women were marginalized.
• **not only … but also …**: Women are **not only** outspoken **but also** involved.
With other verbs: Women **not only** faced discrimination **but** they **also** had no access to education.

# Linking words of CONCESSION / CONTRAST (to show an unexpected idea)
• **but / yet**: The situation is bad, **but** many associations are working to improve it.
• **However, / Nevertheless,** + new sentence: Globalization helped women. **However**, they are still seen as inferior in some societies.
• **whereas / while**: contrast between two ideas in one sentence.
• **although / though / even though + clause**: **Although** women were marginalized, they contributed to the economy.
• **despite / in spite of + noun or gerund**: **Despite** facing discrimination, many women build great careers. / **In spite of** the difficulties, …
• **despite the fact that + clause**

# Key concepts
• **culture**: the way of life of a group of people: customs, beliefs, language and traditions
• **value**: a principle or belief that is important to people
• **cultural values**: the shared principles of a culture

# Cultural values
• **tolerance**: respecting other people's opinions and beliefs (opposite: **intolerance**)
• **coexistence**: living together in harmony with different customs
• **cooperation**: helping one another, working together towards the same goal (opposite: individuality)
• **hospitality**: generous and friendly behaviour towards guests (opposite: unfriendliness)
• **altruism**: caring about the needs of other people; selflessness (opposite: **selfishness**)
• **initiative**: the ability to take the first step, to act before others
• **equality**: treating people the same way (opposite: inequality)
• **equity**: giving people what they need; fair treatment that considers different abilities (opposite: **injustice**)
• **love** (opposite: hatred) · **solidarity** · **generosity** · **respect**

# Word families
• tolerate → tolerance → tolerant · cooperate → cooperation → cooperative
• coexist → coexistence · hospitable → hospitality · altruist → altruism → altruistic

# Phrasal verbs
A **phrasal verb** = verb + particle (preposition/adverb). The meaning is often different from the verb alone: put (place) / put on (wear) / put off (postpone).

# Break
• **break up**: end a relationship · **break down**: stop working (a machine)
• **break into**: enter by force to steal · **break out**: start suddenly (war, fire, disease)

# Look
• **look after**: take care of · **look up**: search for a word in a dictionary
• **look for**: try to find · **look back on**: remember the past
• **look down on**: think you are better than others · **look forward to + -ing**: wait with pleasure

# More phrasal verbs
• **apply for**: ask officially for a job/scholarship · **fill in**: complete a form
• **go through**: experience something difficult · **come across**: meet/find by chance
• **bring about**: cause · **find out**: discover
• **call off**: cancel · **put off**: postpone · **name after**: give someone's name to
• **stand for**: represent (abbreviations) · **call for**: demand publicly
• **drop by**: visit briefly · **pass away**: die
• **carry on**: continue · **bring up**: raise a child
• **lie down**: rest in a lying position · **stay up**: not go to bed

sections.content:
# Reported speech: statements
Reporting verbs: **said (that)**, **told + person (that)**, explained, answered, informed …
When the reporting verb is in the past, the tense goes **one step back**:
• present simple → **past simple**: “I am tired.” → He said (that) he **was** tired.
• present continuous → **past continuous**: “I am working.” → She said she **was working**.
• past simple → **past perfect**: “We finished.” → They said they **had finished**.
• present perfect → **past perfect**: “I have sent it.” → He said he **had sent** it.
• past perfect → **past perfect** (no change)
• am/is/are going to → **was/were going to**

# Commands, requests and advice
• Affirmative: reporting verb + **object + to + infinitive**: “Do your homework!” → My mother told me **to do** my homework.
• Negative: reporting verb + **object + not to + infinitive**: “Don't fight!” → She warned them **not to fight**.
• Reporting verbs: told, ordered, asked, advised, warned, reminded, urged, begged.
• Advice: “You should rest.” → He advised me **to rest**.

# Modals
• will → **would** · can → **could** · may → **might** · must / have to → **had to**

# Time and place
• today → **that day** · now → **then** · yesterday → **the day before / the previous day**
• tomorrow → **the next day / the following day** · next week → **the following week**
• last Monday → **the previous Monday** · ago → **before**
• this → **that** · these → **those** · here → **there**

# Pronouns
Change pronouns to match the speaker: “I love my job.” → She said **she** loved **her** job.

# International organizations
**International organizations** are groups of countries (or people from many countries) working together on global issues such as peace, health, food, human rights and education.

# Organizations and their concerns
• **UN** – United Nations: fostering world peace, stopping conflicts and wars, promoting international cooperation
• **FAO** – Food and Agriculture Organization: fighting hunger, ensuring food security and good nutrition
• **WHO** – World Health Organization: health issues worldwide, fighting dangerous diseases
• **ICRC** – International Committee of the Red Cross: protecting human life and health, protecting victims of armed conflicts, helping victims of natural disasters
• **UNHCR** – United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees: protecting refugees, providing shelter, resettlement in another country
• **AI** – Amnesty International: defending human rights, freeing political prisoners
• **TI** – Transparency International: fighting political and economic corruption
• **UNICEF** – United Nations International Children's Emergency Fund: helping children and mothers in underdeveloped countries
• **UNESCO** – United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization: education, science, culture and communication among nations

# Inside an organization
• **Secretary General**: the head of the organization
• **spokesperson**: the official voice of the organization to the media
• **officials**: people with official positions
• **resolution**: a formal decision or statement
• **constitution**: the fundamental set of principles or laws
• **court**: the place where disputes are resolved
• **headquarters**: the main office (e.g. the WHO headquarters is in Geneva)

sections.title: Wishes & conditional type 3
sections.content:
# Wishes
**Present wish** (regret about a present situation): **wish / if only + past simple** (were for all persons)
• Reality: I don't have a sister. → I **wish** I **had** a sister.
• Reality: I don't live in a big city. → **If only** I **lived** in a big city.
• Reality: Adam can't swim. → Adam wishes he **could** swim.
• Positive ↔ negative: Leila spends too much time online → Leila wishes she **didn't spend** so much time online.

**Past wish** (regret about the past): **wish / if only + past perfect (had + pp)**
• Reality: I didn't revise. → I wish I **had revised** for the exam.
• Reality: I failed the exam. → I wish I **hadn't failed** the exam.

# Conditional type 3
For **impossible / unreal situations in the past** (the past can't be changed).
**Form:** If + **past perfect**, subject + **would have + past participle**
• Reality: I didn't study, so I didn't pass. → If I **had studied** harder, I **would have passed** the exam.
• The if-clause can come second (no comma): He **wouldn't have missed** the train if he **had left** earlier.
• Remember to reverse positive ↔ negative: She didn't wake up early → If she **had woken** up early, she **wouldn't have missed** the bus.

sections.title: Loss of human capital
sections.content:
# Brain drain
**Brain drain** (loss of human capital) is when **skilled professionals** — doctors, engineers, scientists, academics and other **highly educated** people — leave their **country of origin** (often an **underdeveloped / developing** country) to work in a developed **host country**. They seek better opportunities, good **working conditions** or **higher salaries**.
Consequently, the countries of origin **lose** talented people, while host countries **gain** skilled workers.

# Push factors (bad conditions that force people to emigrate)
• low wages and incomes · bad living conditions · bad working conditions
• lack of advanced technology and research facilities
• bad quality of the educational system · wars and conflicts

# Pull factors (good conditions that attract people)
• higher wages · advanced technology and research facilities
• better working conditions · political stability
• intellectual freedom · a promising future · better quality of life

# Useful words
• **to emigrate** (leave your country) / **to immigrate** (come into a new country)
• **emigrant / immigrant / migration** · **skilled professionals** · **human capital**
• **brain gain** (for the host country) · **to retain talent** (keep skilled people)

sections.content:
# Relative pronouns
• **who** → people (subject of the verb): A lawyer is a person **who** helps people.
• **whom** → people (object of the verb, formal): The woman **whom** he interviewed was hired.
• **which** → things, animals and ideas: I like the present **which** my sister sent.
• **that** → people or things (in defining clauses, informal)
• **whose** → possession: The boy **whose** father is a doctor had an accident.
• **where** → places: This is the town **where** the president was born.
• **when** → time: I'll never forget the day **when** I got married.

# Joining sentences
• This is Anna's father. He gave me a phone. → This is Anna's father **who** gave me a phone.
• This is the shop. I bought my glasses from this shop. → This is the shop **where** I bought my glasses.
• The woman's husband is dead. She is called a widow. → A woman **whose** husband is dead is called a widow.

# Watch out
• Don't repeat the pronoun: ✗ the photos which he took **them** → ✓ the photos which he took.
• After a preposition, use **whom** or **which**: the professor **with whom** I was talking.

sections.content:
# Expressing regret
We express regret when we feel sorry about something that happened (or didn't happen) in the past.

# Form: wish / if only + past perfect (had + past participle)
• Reality: I emigrated to the USA, but I can't find a job. → I **wish I had stayed** in my home country.
• Reality: The government didn't accept our demands. → **If only** they **had accepted** our demands.
• Reality: I didn't apply for the scholarship. → I **wish I had applied** for the scholarship.

# Other expressions
• I regret + -ing: I **regret leaving** my country.
• I should have + pp: I **should have studied** harder.
• It's a pity (that) … / What a shame!

# Responding to someone's regret
• Don't worry, you'll have another chance. · It's not too late. · I know how you feel.
